deck.title: Types of Business & Sources of Finance

front_blocks.md: Define a **sole trader**.

back_blocks.md: A **sole trader** is a person who **owns and controls** a business on their own. No formal permission is needed to set one up, which makes it the **simplest** business form to start.

cards.front_md: Define a **sole trader**.
cards.back_md: A **sole trader** is a person who **owns and controls** a business on their own. No formal permission is needed to set one up, which makes it the **simplest** business form to start.

front_blocks.md: Complete the sentence about who runs a sole trader's business:
A sole trader may `\_\_\_\_\_\_` other people to help run the business, but is still the only `\_\_\_\_\_\_` of it.

back_blocks.md: The completed sentence is:
A sole trader may **employ** other people to help run the business, but is still the only **owner** of it.

front_blocks.md: Give two advantages of operating as a sole trader.

back_blocks.md: A sole trader:

- keeps **all** of the profit the business makes
- can make **decisions quickly**, without needing to consult anyone else
- has **simpler** book-keeping and accounting to do than larger business forms

front_blocks.md: Define **unlimited liability**.

back_blocks.md: **Unlimited liability** means the owner and the business are treated as **one entity**, with no legal separation between them. If the business cannot pay its debts, the owner's **personal possessions** can be taken to pay them.

front_blocks.md: Give two disadvantages of operating as a sole trader.

back_blocks.md: A sole trader:

- bears **all** of the responsibility for any losses the business makes
- has **no one** to share the workload or the decisions with
- is **limited** in the amount of capital they can put into the business
- may earn **nothing** during periods of illness or holiday

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A sole trader must make their financial statements available to the public.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
A sole trader's financial statements are **private**. There is no requirement to publish them, so competitors cannot see how the business is performing.

front_blocks.md: Why is a sole trader usually limited in how much capital they can put into the business?

back_blocks.md: There is **no one else** to contribute, so the capital is limited to whatever the **single owner** can provide. A business with more than one owner can draw on more than one person's resources.

front_blocks.md: Define a **partnership**.

back_blocks.md: A **partnership** is a business owned by **two or more people** who run it together with the aim of making a **profit**. The partners are the owners of the business, not its employees.

cards.front_md: Define a **partnership**.

front_blocks.md: Give two advantages of operating as a partnership.

back_blocks.md: Partners:

- can raise **more capital**, because every partner contributes to it
- bring different **skills and expertise** to the business
- **share the risks** of running it
- can **cover for each other** during illness and holidays

A partnership normally consists of between two and `\_\_\_\_\_\_` partners.

back_blocks.md: The completed sentence is:
A partnership normally consists of between two and **twenty** partners.

front_blocks.md: Give two disadvantages of operating as a partnership.

back_blocks.md: Partners:

- must **share** the profits between them
- may **disagree** with one another about how to run the business
- may take **longer to reach decisions**, because their opinions differ

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A partnership can be formed by a sole trader who wants to expand the business.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
A sole trader who wants to **grow** can take on a partner rather than starting a new business. Two or more sole traders can also **combine** their money and assets to form a partnership together.

front_blocks.md: One partner runs up a debt on behalf of the business. Who is responsible for repaying it?

back_blocks.md: **All** of the partners are responsible, not only the partner who created the debt. Each partner is therefore exposed to the decisions the others make.

front_blocks.md: Define a **limited company**.

back_blocks.md: A **limited company** is a business owned by a group of people, whose ownership is divided into **shares**. The people who buy those shares are the **shareholders**.

cards.front_md: Define a **limited company**.
cards.back_md: A **limited company** is a business owned by a group of people, whose ownership is divided into **shares**. The people who buy those shares are the **shareholders**.

front_blocks.md: What is the difference between a private and a public limited company?

back_blocks.md: The difference is **who can buy the shares**. Anyone can buy shares in a **public** limited company (PLC), while shares in a **private** limited company (Ltd) are **not sold publicly**.

cards.front_md: What is the difference between a private and a public limited company?
cards.back_md: The difference is **who can buy the shares**. Anyone can buy shares in a **public** limited company (PLC), while shares in a **private** limited company (Ltd) are **not sold publicly**.

front_blocks.md: Complete the sentence about the value of a share:
The monetary value of a share is called its **nominal** value, also known as its **face** value or its `\_\_\_\_\_\_` value.

back_blocks.md: The completed sentence is:
The monetary value of a share is called its **nominal** value, also known as its **face** value or its **par** value.

front_blocks.md: Define **limited liability**.

back_blocks.md: **Limited liability** means the company is a **separate entity** from its owners, so the owners are liable only for the amount they have **invested**. If the company fails, a shareholder loses their investment but nothing more.

front_blocks.md: Give two advantages of operating as a limited company.

back_blocks.md: A limited company:

- can usually raise **more capital** than a sole trader or a partnership
- gives its owners **limited liability**, which the other business forms do not

front_blocks.md: Define a **dividend**.

back_blocks.md: A **dividend** is the reward a **shareholder** receives for investing money in a limited company. It is paid as a proportion of the **face value** of the shares they hold.

cards.front_md: Define a **dividend**.
cards.back_md: A **dividend** is the reward a **shareholder** receives for investing money in a limited company. It is paid as a proportion of the **face value** of the shares they hold.

front_blocks.md: A shareholder holds 4000 shares and the dividend is \$0.05 per share. What dividend do they receive?

back_blocks.md: The shareholder receives **\$200**. The dividend paid is **number of shares × dividend per share**, so 4000 × \$0.05 = \$200.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A limited company must pay its shareholders a dividend every year.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Dividends are paid out of the **profits** the company makes, so there may be nothing to pay in a year when it does not make one. A shareholder's return is **not guaranteed**.

front_blocks.md: Give two disadvantages of operating as a limited company.

back_blocks.md: A limited company:

- must meet **more legal requirements**, including audits and publishing its financial statements
- **costs more to set up** than a sole trader business or a partnership

front_blocks.md: Define a **trading business**.

back_blocks.md: A **trading business** buys goods and then **sells them on** without changing them. Grocery stores and car dealerships are examples.

cards.front_md: Define a **trading business**.
cards.back_md: A **trading business** buys goods and then **sells them on** without changing them. Grocery stores and car dealerships are examples.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
One business can be a trading business and a manufacturing business at the same time.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Many businesses do a **mix** of the three. A sandwich shop that makes its own sandwiches but buys in crisps and drinks to sell is both **manufacturing** and **trading**.

front_blocks.md: Define a **service business**.

back_blocks.md: A **service business** provides a **service** rather than buying or selling goods. Insurance companies, accountants, travel agents and hairdressers are examples.

cards.front_md: Define a **service business**.

front_blocks.md: Does a business's legal form, such as sole trader or limited company, decide whether it is trading, service or manufacturing?

back_blocks.md: **Any** legal form can be a trading, service or manufacturing business. A sole trader can be a manufacturer, and a limited company can be a service business.

front_blocks.md: Define a **manufacturing business**.

back_blocks.md: A **manufacturing business** **produces** the goods it sells, rather than buying them ready-made. Clothes factories and food factories are examples.

cards.front_md: Define a **manufacturing business**.

front_blocks.md: What is the difference between a short-term and a long-term source of finance?

back_blocks.md: Short-term sources are repaid **within a year**, while long-term sources are repaid **over several years**. An overdraft and trade credit are short-term, whereas a bank loan is long-term.

cards.front_md: What is the difference between a short-term and a long-term source of finance?
cards.back_md: Short-term sources are repaid **within a year**, while long-term sources are repaid **over several years**. An overdraft and trade credit are short-term, whereas a bank loan is long-term.

front_blocks.md: Define a **bank overdraft**.

back_blocks.md: A **bank overdraft** lets a business spend **more money than it has** in its bank account. Interest is charged only on the amount actually used, and the funds are available **immediately**.

cards.front_md: Define a **bank overdraft**.
cards.back_md: A **bank overdraft** lets a business spend **more money than it has** in its bank account. Interest is charged only on the amount actually used, and the funds are available **immediately**.

front_blocks.md: Give one drawback of relying on a bank overdraft to finance a business.

back_blocks.md: An overdraft:

- carries **high** interest rates
- is usually limited to a fairly **small** amount
- can be relied on too heavily, so the business never clears it

front_blocks.md: Define **trade credit**.

back_blocks.md: **Trade credit** is where a business receives goods or assets now and **pays for them at a later date**. It is usually **interest-free** if the business pays on time.

cards.front_md: Define **trade credit**.
cards.back_md: **Trade credit** is where a business receives goods or assets now and **pays for them at a later date**. It is usually **interest-free** if the business pays on time.

front_blocks.md: How does taking trade credit improve a business's working capital?

back_blocks.md: The cash stays in the business for **longer**, because payment is delayed. That leaves more money available for **day-to-day** trading in the meantime.

cards.front_md: How does taking trade credit improve a business's working capital?

front_blocks.md: Define a **debenture**.

back_blocks.md: A **debenture** is a long-term loan made to a **limited company** by an investor. The company pays **interest** each year and repays the full amount on an **agreed future date**.

cards.front_md: Define a **debenture**.
cards.back_md: A **debenture** is a long-term loan made to a **limited company** by an investor. The company pays **interest** each year and repays the full amount on an **agreed future date**.

front_blocks.md: What is the main difference between leasing an asset and buying it on hire purchase?

back_blocks.md: The difference is **ownership**. Under **leasing** the business rents the asset and never owns it, while under **hire purchase** it pays a deposit and instalments and **owns the asset** once the final payment is made.

cards.front_md: What is the main difference between leasing an asset and buying it on hire purchase?
cards.back_md: The difference is **ownership**. Under **leasing** the business rents the asset and never owns it, while under **hire purchase** it pays a deposit and instalments and **owns the asset** once the final payment is made.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Money put into a business by its own owner counts as a source of finance.

back_blocks.md: **True.**

The owner's own **capital** is a source of finance, and it carries no interest and never has to be repaid. It is only available to sole traders and partnerships, and the owner loses it if the business fails.

front_blocks.md: Give two advantages to a business of raising finance through a bank loan.

back_blocks.md: A bank loan:

- makes **large amounts** of cash available
- has **regular, fixed** repayments, which are easy to budget for
- leaves the owners in **full control** of the business
- spreads the cost of an asset over **several years**

front_blocks.md: Give two disadvantages to a business of raising finance through a bank loan.

back_blocks.md: A bank loan:

- carries **interest**, which adds to the total cost
- must be repaid whether the business makes a **profit or a loss**
- may require the business to offer an asset as **security**
